A mutable field needs a declared type: the generated setter has to
convert an incoming value into something, and only the declaration
says what. A read-only field needs none.

Rust reads its state from the struct and its behaviour from the
inherent impl. "fn new() -> Self" is the constructor and is not a
member; "impl Default" is accepted in its place.

Swift, from the class shown here:

    private let tacInstance = Companion()
    let tac: [String: TacMember] = [
        "count": .field({ tacInstance.count },
                        { tacInstance.count = $0 as? Int ?? tacInstance.count }),
        "doubled": .method({ _ in tacInstance.doubled() }),
    ]

Declaring the table yourself replaces this entirely.

features.title: REST handlers
features.summary: A yon.* file defines an endpoint. An ordinary value becomes a JSON response; an explicit descriptor sets status and headers. The class declares its layer with @Controller, which Tachyon checks against where the file sits.

<?php
#[Controller]
class ProductsController
{
    public static function GET(YonRequest $request): YonResponse
    {
        return YonResponse::json(json_encode(['products' => ['anvil']]));
    }

    public static function POST(YonRequest $request): YonResponse
    {
        // The body is raw text, so it is decoded rather than assumed.
        $sent = json_decode($request->body(), true) ?? [];
        return YonResponse::json(json_encode(['created' => $sent]))->status(201);
    }
}

features.title: Eight server languages
features.summary: A Yon handler declares its layer, so Yon runs the languages whose syntax can carry that declaration: JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Java, C#, Kotlin, PHP and Rust. Two have a built-in adapter, four are compiled and cached on first use, and none of them says how it is started — Yon knows how to start each of the eight.

<?php
// No shebang and no envelope. Tachyon appends the protocol runtime after this
// file, so the handler is a class and its methods — nothing here reads stdin
// or writes stdout. PHP resolves an attribute lazily, so #[Controller] needs
// no import.
#[Controller]
class EchoController
{
    public static function POST(YonRequest $request): YonResponse
    {
        $sent = json_decode($request->body(), true) ?? [];
        return YonResponse::json(json_encode(['echoed' => $sent]))->status(201);
    }
}

resolution
files.code:
How a handler is started

  yon.js, yon.ts    a built-in adapter, on a runtime that reads it
  yon.py            a built-in adapter
  yon.php           php, with the protocol runtime appended
  yon.java          JEP 330 single-file source launch
  yon.rs            rustc, with a proc-macro crate for the attributes
  yon.kt            kotlinc, run with java -jar
  yon.cs            a generated project, built with dotnet

No shebang. Yon runs eight languages and knows how to start each,
so a handler declares its methods and nothing about its own
execution. A shebang was the right answer while Yon ran any
language — there is no table of every interpreter in the world —
but a bounded set is a table, and one Tachyon owns rather than
every handler repeating.

Which JavaScript, though, is the project's to choose:

  TACHYON_JAVASCRIPT_RUNTIME=$(command -v bun) ty start
  TACHYON_PYTHON_RUNTIME=/usr/bin/python3.13 ty start

It matters for more than speed. A yon.js or yon.ts that declares
@Controller needs a runtime that transpiles a decorator: Bun and
Deno do, and Node — the default — never will.

Compiled handlers are cached under .tachyon/handlers/<source digest>.

Go, Ruby, Perl, C and C++ are not Yon languages: none of them can
carry the annotation a handler declares its layer with. They are
reached through @Relay instead.

features.title: Relaying to Go, Ruby and the rest
features.summary: Yon runs the eight languages that can declare a layer, which leaves Go, Ruby, Elixir and the rest with no way in. They are still programs, though, and a program that speaks Handler Protocol v1 on standard input and output is exactly what Yon spawns anyway — so @Relay on a method makes it a proxy for one. The command sits on the declaration because it is metadata about the method, not part of its work. A handler written before Yon narrowed runs unchanged.

files.name: server/delegates/report.rb
files.code:
# A Ruby program, not a Tachyon handler: Yon does not run
# Ruby, because Ruby cannot carry a class annotation and a
# handler declares its layer with one.
#
# It does not have to be a handler. It reads one Handler
# Protocol v1 request on stdin and writes one response on
# stdout — which is what a Yon handler in any language
# already did, so one written before Yon narrowed runs here
# unchanged.
require 'json'

request = JSON.parse($stdin.read) rescue {}
puts JSON.generate({
  'status' => 200,
  'headers' => { 'content-type' => ['application/json'] },
  'body' => JSON.generate({
    'language' => 'Ruby',
    'route' => request['route']
  })
})

files.name: relaying
files.code:
Relaying to a language Yon does not run

  Yon runs the eight languages that can declare a layer.
  Everything else is still a program, so @Relay spawns it
  and speaks the protocol at it. The annotation is written
  in the language doing the relaying, so nothing has to be
  installed on the other side.

  Rust        #[Relay("ruby", "server/delegates/report.rb")]
  JavaScript  @Relay('ruby', 'server/delegates/report.rb')
  TypeScript  @Relay('ruby', 'server/delegates/report.rb')
  Python      @Relay("ruby", "server/delegates/report.rb")
  Java        @Relay({"ruby", "server/delegates/report.rb"})
  Kotlin      @Relay("ruby", "server/delegates/report.rb")
  C#          [Relay("ruby", "server/delegates/report.rb")]
  PHP         #[Relay('ruby', 'server/delegates/report.rb')]

  Four of them carry it out themselves: Rust rewrites the
  body, and JavaScript, TypeScript and Python return the
  function that replaces the one it sits on. In Java,
  Kotlin, C# and PHP an annotation is inert, so the
  dispatch reads it back and the body those languages
  oblige you to write is never called.

  The relayed status and headers travel, not only the
  body. A program that cannot be started answers 502 with
  the reason, because it is a program on the host and "it
  is not installed" is not otherwise visible.

  For a command not known until the request arrives, call
  relay(command, request) instead.

  @Delegate stays the layer that owns handed-off work.
  @Relay is what a method does; @Delegate is where the
  code lives.

features.title: Middleware
features.summary: One middleware source at the project root runs before every request and again after the response, so it can refuse a request, and adjust or replace what a handler produced.

files.name: middleware.js
middleware.php
files.code:
<?php
// Middleware speaks the protocol a handler does, so it may be written in any
// language Yon runs. A 204 continues; any other status answers the request
// without reaching the route.
class Middleware
{
    public static function before(array $request): array
    {
        $token = $request['headers']['authorization'][0] ?? '';
        if (str_starts_with($request['route'], '/private') && $token !== 'let-me-in') {
            return ['status' => 401, 'body' => 'unauthorized'];
        }
        return ['status' => 204];
    }
}

files.name: middleware.py
files.code:
import json, sys

request = json.loads(sys.stdin.read())
authorized = request.get("headers", {}).get("authorization")

# 204 continues to the route handler; anything else answers the request.
print(json.dumps(
    {"status": 204, "headers": {}, "body": ""} if authorized
    else {"status": 401, "headers": {"content-type": "text/plain"}, "body": "Unauthorized"}
))

files.name: languages
files.code:
Which languages middleware is written in

  middleware.js   the JavaScript adapter
  middleware.ts   the same adapter, on a runtime that reads TypeScript
  middleware.py   the Python adapter
  middleware.php  php, speaking the protocol itself

Not the compiled four. Middleware answers `before` and `after`
rather than an HTTP method, and the protocol runtime Tachyon
appends to a compiled handler dispatches on the method — it would
find neither, and write a 405 after whatever the middleware had
already written. So middleware in Java, Kotlin, C# or Rust is not
supported rather than merely undocumented.

PHP is on this list for the same reason it is excluded from the
handler runtime: it speaks the protocol itself, as every handler
did before handlers stopped having to.

features.title: Declared route contracts
features.summary: A route declares what it accepts and answers in an OPTIONS.schema.json beside its handler, in CHEX schematics. A request is described the way one arrives — headers, path parameters, body — and CHEX enforces every declared part before the handler runs.

files.name: server/routes/secure/_id/OPTIONS.schema.json
enforced
files.code:
$ curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer supersecret' /secure/42
200  {"id":"42","seen":true}

$ curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer supersecret' /secure/abc
400  {"error":"RegEx pattern fails for property 'id' …","part":"parameters"}

$ curl /secure/42
400  {"error":"Property 'authorization' cannot be null …","part":"headers"}

$ curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer supersecret' -H 'X-Whatever: 1' /secure/42
200  # an undeclared header is not a reason to reject anything

# CHEX is the validator. Responses stay in three buckets — ok (2xx),
# clientError (4xx), serverError (5xx) — rather than numeric codes:
# any 2xx must satisfy 'ok', so there is no question of what a status
# the contract never listed should mean.

files.code:
Which languages a stream is written in

  yon.js, yon.ts   an async generator
  yon.py           a generator
  yon.php          a generator, framed by the prelude
  yon.kt           a Sequence, framed by the prelude
  yon.cs           an IEnumerable or IAsyncEnumerable, framed
                   by the prelude

Six of the eight. A stream is a handler that answers more than
once, and `yield` is how a handler says so in its own words. The
two built-in adapters hold a generator open across frames, and
PHP, Kotlin and C# now do the same without one.

Java and Rust are the two left out, and deliberately: neither has
a generator, so `yield` is not what an author would write there.
@Stream in either is refused with TY2014 rather than accepted and
quietly ignored, and a route that must stream can be one of the
six — or reach the rest through @Relay.

One thing follows from the annotation: a streaming yon.js needs
Bun or Deno, because Node will never transpile a decorator. Every
other language needs nothing.

features.title: Layer stereotypes
features.summary: A server class declares its layer — @Controller, @Service, @Repository, @Client, @Delegate — and Tachyon checks the declaration against where the file sits, what it reaches, what the class is named, and, for a controller, what it declares. Not dependency injection: a handler is one process per request, so nothing an injector built would outlive the response. What they buy is the architecture written down and enforced.

refused
files.code:
error[TY2008]: 'server/services/orders.py' declares @Repository
               but is not under server/repositories/.

error[TY2009]: 'server/repositories/orders.py' is a @Repository
               and reaches server/services/.

error[TY2011]: 'server/routes/orders/yon.py' declares @Controller
               on 'Orders', which does not end in Controller.

error[TY2012]: 'server/routes/orders/yon.py' declares 'score()'
               on the controller 'OrdersController'.

A layer may reach a deeper one and never a shallower one.

  @Controller   server/routes         a request in, a response out
  @Service      server/services       owns a decision
  @Repository   server/repositories   owns storage
  @Client       server/clients        owns one outbound call
  @Delegate     server/delegates      owns work handed elsewhere

The bottom three are peers, not a stack.

A stereotyped class is named for its layer, because the name is
visible at every call site and the annotation only at the
declaration. And a controller declares HTTP methods and nothing
else: the dispatch finds the method by name, so a helper beside
GET is never reached through a route. It reads as working and
never runs.

files.name: languages
files.code:
One name in eight languages, in each language’s own bracket:

  Java, Kotlin    @Controller
  C#              [Controller]
  PHP, Rust       #[Controller]
  Python          @Controller
  JavaScript, TS  @Controller

Not Go or Ruby. Go has no annotation syntax — a struct tag is
metadata on a field rather than on a type, and a //go: directive is
a comment. Ruby has none either.

No import is needed, and each language is given them the way it
can take them. The JavaScript and Python adapters put the
stereotypes in scope before loading the handler. Rust gets a `use`
prepended, because its attributes are a procedural macro crate
built and linked alongside. Java, Kotlin and C# declare them in
the protocol runtime Tachyon supplies, which for the first two is
appended after the handler — declaring them in both places is a
redeclaration error, which is how that was found. PHP resolves an
attribute lazily and needs no declaration at all.

features.title: What a companion reaches
features.summary: A compiled companion is linked into the host process, so the platform’s own SDK is simply there — AppKit, the Android SDK, the .NET base class library. There is no capability vocabulary in between: a tray, a window or a notification belongs to the platform, and a fixed list of verbs could only ever be the subset the framework had got round to.

client/pages/tac.cs     the .NET base class library
client/pages/tac.rs     the Rust standard library, on three desktops

The host implements one channel and no verbs — companion.invoke:
the page asks its companion for a member, and the companion answers. Everything a
platform can do is the companion's to reach directly.

features.title: One rendering everywhere
features.summary: A native build hosts the application’s own web bundle, so a desktop or mobile app renders exactly what the browser renders. Matching a platform’s own look is a choice you make in your UI layer, with whichever cross-platform kit you already use.

features.summary: The page asks a companion for a member; tacPublish is the other direction. features.summary: Every failure carries a stable TY code, a bounded message and an actionable help line. A code is a contract: an operator alerting on TY2105 is looking at the machine, and one reading TY2012 is looking at the code.

features.title: Deterministic builds
features.summary: A repeated build is byte-identical, and an unchanged route is reused against a verified digest. A failed build leaves the last good output in place.

features.title: A view is not a document
features.summary: A tac.html is the page’s content. The compiler writes the document around it, so a doctype, <html>, <head> or <body> in a view is TY1307 — a head authored there is one the emitted document cannot merge with its own.

features.summary: Title, description, canonical and social tags are declared per route in tac.config.js. The module already knows the route list — it is what generates the sitemap — so metadata belongs there rather than repeated in every template.

features.title: Which companion answers a target
features.summary: A companion language compiles for the targets whose toolchain and SDK it belongs to. Building a target no declared companion reaches is TY1010, not a silent omission — an application that starts up and does nothing is a worse answer than a build that refuses.

files.name: matrix
files.code:
tac.js, tac.ts   web, and every native target
tac.rs           macos, windows, linux
tac.swift        macos, ios
tac.kt           android
tac.cs           windows

A route may declare several. When more than one reaches the target
being built, the platform's own language wins over Rust, and only
the winner is compiled — no two platform languages reach the same
target, so the choice is never a tie broken by declaration order.

features.title: Errors that clear themselves
features.summary: A failed rebuild shows its diagnostics over the open page. The next rebuild that succeeds removes them — the overlay tracks the state of the code, not the history of it, so a fixed error stops being on screen without a reload.

files.name: sequence
files.code:
1  save a broken view     -> overlay appears, naming the TY code
2  keep typing            -> overlay updates in place
3  save a working view    -> overlay is removed, page hot-updates

No reload at any step. The page that recovers is the page that
was open, with its scroll position and focus intact.

features.title: What a page may do to its window
features.summary: A native window is declared in manifest.json — the file a PWA already ships — and what a page may do to that window is granted there too. Nothing by default. A control that was not granted is not generated into the host, so there is no code to reach rather than a check that refuses.

files.name: manifest.json
client/pages/tac.js
client/pages/tac.html
files.code: Report

files.name: grants
files.code:
What a page may do to its window

  close        dismiss the window
  fullscreen   toggle full screen
  maximize     zoom to fill the display
  minimize     send to the dock or taskbar
  resize       set width and height
  title        set the window title

Empty by default. Nothing is granted unless it is listed, and a
control that is not listed is not generated into the host at all
— there is no code to reach, not a check that says no.

Electron hands a privileged process the whole window and trusts
the application. Tauri gates each call behind a permission in a
capabilities dialect of its own. This is the same default-deny,
declared in the file the application already ships: manifest.json
is where a PWA already says its name, its icons and where it
starts, and a manifest carrying members a browser does not know
is still a valid manifest.

An unknown control is refused at build time, naming the six.

features.title: Handler isolation
features.summary: A handler is one bounded process per request by default. A deployment that wants more than process isolation sets YON_ISOLATION=firecracker and each request is handed to a microVM control program instead — the same handler, the same protocol, the same build.

files.name: isolation
files.code:
How a handler runs

  YON_ISOLATION=process       one supervised child process per
                              request. The default.

  YON_ISOLATION=firecracker   hand each request to a Firecracker
                              control program instead.

    YON_FIRECRACKER_DRIVER      the control program to run
    YON_FIRECRACKER_POOL        how many microVMs to keep
    YON_FIRECRACKER_VCPUS       vCPUs per microVM
    YON_FIRECRACKER_MEMORY_MIB  memory per microVM
    YON_FIRECRACKER_EGRESS      what a handler may reach

Read from the environment rather than a config file, because
which isolation a deployment wants is a property of where it
runs, not of the source — the same build runs either way.

An invalid or half-declared policy fails as TY2010 before a
handler runs, rather than falling back to something weaker than
what was asked for.

features.title: Serving what was published
features.summary: `ty start` serves a built bundle and never rebuilds. Everything that differs between deployments — the interface, the port, which JavaScript runtime runs a handler — is read from the environment, so the artifact staging serves is byte-identical to the one production serves.

files.name: environment
files.code:
Serving a built bundle

  YON_HOST        interface to bind, or YON_HOSTNAME
  YON_PORT        TCP port; zero takes an ephemeral one
  YON_DIST_PATH   where the built bundle is

  TACHYON_JAVASCRIPT_RUNTIME   node, bun or deno
  TACHYON_PYTHON_RUNTIME       the CPython to use
  TAC_CACHE_DIR                where the standalone runtime cache lives

`ty start` serves what was published and never rebuilds, so
everything that varies between deployments is in the environment
rather than in the artifact. The bundle a staging host serves is
byte-identical to the one production serves.

The runtime variables matter for more than speed: a yon.js or
yon.ts that declares @Controller needs a runtime that transpiles
a decorator, and Node — the default — never will.

features.title: What a project looks like
features.summary: One directory tree, two halves. Client routes are directories holding a tac.html; server layers are directories a class declares itself into. Everything else is a convention with no rule attached.

files.name: layout
files.code:
What `ty init` lays out

  client/
    pages/        one directory per route, holding a tac.html
    components/   a two-level path, `<product-card>`
    shared/       published as-is, imported by both halves

  server/
    routes/       @Controller — a request in, a response out
    services/     @Service — owns a decision
    repositories/ @Repository — owns storage
    clients/      @Client — owns one outbound call
    delegates/    @Delegate — owns work handed elsewhere
    stereotypes/  the annotation declarations, for languages
                  that need them declared
    vendor/       third-party code, checked in
    config/       configuration a handler reads
    data/         files a handler reads or writes

  manifest.json   name, icons, and the native window
  tac.config.js   identity, page metadata, build hooks

The five layer directories are the contract: a class declares
which one it is in, and Tachyon checks the declaration against
where the file sits. The rest are conventions with no rule
attached — they exist so a project does not have to invent a name
for the same thing twice.
